title: class, constructor, extends, and super
hook: The class keyword looks like C# or Java, but under the hood JavaScript still wires prototype links and constructor functions. Interviews test whether you know the sugar versus the runtime mechanics.

blocks.text: A **class declaration** is syntactic sugar over constructor functions and prototype objects. `class AuthHandler { constructor(id) { this.id = id; } parse(raw) { return raw; } }` creates a function `AuthHandler` with a `.prototype` object holding `parse`. **`extends`** sets the subclass prototype's [[Prototype]] to the superclass prototype. **`super`** in a constructor calls the parent constructor; in methods it refers to the parent's prototype for `super.method()` calls.

entries.plainDefinition: class syntax that desugars to functions and prototype wiring — no separate class type in the engine.
entries.example: `typeof AuthHandler === 'function'` even when declared with class.

entries.plainDefinition: Special method that runs on new. Initializes own properties on this.
Sets up prototype chain between subclass and superclass prototypes and provides super binding.
In constructors: calls parent constructor. In methods: parent prototype for super calls.

blocks.text: Teams use `class` for readable hierarchies — React components, domain models, test doubles. TypeScript compiles classes to the same prototype pattern. When debugging, stack traces show class names because constructors retain the `name` property. But **private fields**, **static** blocks, and **extends** have spec rules that differ from C# — especially around `super()` order and `this` before `super()` in derived constructors.

blocks.title: Classes are not hoisted like functions
blocks.body: Class declarations are in the temporal dead zone until initialized — referencing `AuthHandler` before its declaration throws ReferenceError. Function declarations hoist.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Create object with correct [[Prototype]]
items.body: The runtime creates an object whose [[Prototype]] is `ClassName.prototype`.

items.title: Call constructor with this bound
items.body: The constructor runs with `this` as the new object. In derived classes, you must call `super(...)` before using `this`.

items.title: Return the object
items.body: If the constructor returns a non-object, that return value becomes the result of `new`. Returning an object replaces the default instance — rare but valid.

items.title: Methods live on prototype
items.body: Instance methods are non-enumerable properties on `ClassName.prototype`, not copied per instance.

snippet.explanation: Line 1–6: constructor function plus prototype method — the pre-ES6 pattern. Line 9–11: extends adjusts both instance and static prototype chains — why Lti inherits static methods from AuthHandler.

blocks.title: Using this before super() in derived constructor
blocks.body: In a derived class constructor, accessing `this` before `super()` throws ReferenceError. C# allows different ordering rules with field initializers — do not assume parity.

blocks.title: Arrow functions as class fields versus prototype methods
blocks.body: Class field `handler = () => {}` creates an own property per instance (lexical this). Prototype method shares one function. Memory and binding differ — pick intentionally.

blocks.text: **Class bodies** are evaluated in strict mode. **Method definitions** on the prototype are non-enumerable and use `.name` inference. **extends** copies static own properties and sets `Symbol.hasInstance` behavior on the subclass. **super** inside methods uses the **home object** algorithm — it is not just AuthHandler.prototype.parse; it respects the current class's [[Prototype]] slot in the inheritance tree. **Returning from constructor**: if you `return { ok: true }` from a class constructor, `new` yields that object instead of the instance — breaks instanceof expectations. TypeScript **parameter properties** and **abstract** classes do not exist in emitted JS unless you emulate them.

snippet.explanation: Line 4: returning a plain object from constructor overrides default instance. Line 8–10: new does not produce CacheEntry instance — rare but valid JS behavior unlike C# constructors.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying class introduces a new object model separate from prototypes — it does not. Claiming TypeScript private fields exist at runtime without # emit — they do not. Assuming super works like C# base in all contexts — JS super is tied to prototype slots and has restrictions in arrow functions in some cases.

interviewTakeaways: class desugars to constructor functions plus prototype objects — typeof MyClass is function.
extends links Lti.prototype's [[Prototype]] to AuthHandler.prototype; super calls parent constructor or prototype methods.
Derived constructors must call super() before using this — ReferenceError otherwise.

60s: class is sugar over prototypes. new creates object, runs constructor, methods on prototype. extends sets chain. super in ctor calls parent; in methods calls parent prototype. Static methods live on the constructor function. Not the same as C# CLR types.
Follow-up: difference between prototype method and class field arrow function for this binding.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'JavaScript classes are like C# classes at runtime.' Strong: they are functions with prototype links — no CLR metadata or nominal typing.
Using this before super in derived constructor — throws ReferenceError.
Class field arrows for every method — allocates per instance; use prototype methods when lexical this is not required.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS access modifiers and parameter properties erase; only # private survives as real runtime privacy in modern emit.
C# base(...) chains before derived body; JS requires super() before this — similar intent, different rules.
